answer: Before 1922 there was no modern census: earlier figures are estimates, some probably undercounts. For 1914 estimates give about 689,000 people in all, with Jews put at 60,000 to 94,000. The 1922 census recorded 757,182 people, 83,794 of them Jews; the last, in 1931, recorded 1,035,821, with 174,610 Jews. By the end of 1946 the UN committee estimated the settled population at about 1,846,000, 1,203,000 of them Arabs and 608,000 Jews; its own table puts the Jewish share at 12.91 percent in 1922 and 32.96 percent in 1946. About 376,000 Jewish immigrants were recorded from 1920 to 1946, most of the Jewish growth. British and UN inquiries put Arab growth almost entirely down to births over deaths, but Arab immigration was not fully recorded, and a minority view says it mattered more. Every count after 1922 is one set of Mandate statistics. The land was inhabited, mostly by Arabs.

facts.text: Population figures before the first British census (1922) are estimates. The 1922 census report says the Ottoman counts existed to list men liable for military service or to impose taxes. The demographer Justin McCarthy writes that the Ottomans consistently undercounted women and children (a statement about the empire as a whole, not Palestine alone). The demographer Sergio DellaPergola labels his own series for 1800 to 1914 'rough estimates'. A Cambridge article re-examining an actual 1849 Ottoman count of Nablus (20,000, against the 8,000-9,000 usually cited) says it raises serious doubts about commonly accepted figures, so the older outside estimates may be too low. The Mandate's Survey says no data are available on the size of the population before the British occupation.

facts.text: The UN Special Committee on Palestine (UNSCOP) estimated the settled population at the end of 1946 at about 1,846,000: 1,203,000 Arabs, 608,000 Jews and 35,000 others, and warned that such estimates carry a margin of error that grows as the census year recedes. Its vital records cover the whole population except the small Bedouin group living as nomads. On UNSCOP's own table, on one basis, the Jewish share was 12.91 percent in 1922 and 32.96 percent in 1946; that 1922 base (649,048) is not the census total (757,182), so the table is compared with itself and not with the census. The figures come from the Mandate government's statistician, so UNSCOP, the Survey and the Anglo-American Committee repeat one set of British statistics rather than confirming it independently.

facts.text: The Survey's statisticians made no allowance for illegal immigration before 1939, so the official migration counts are incomplete. The demographer Roberto Bachi, quoted second-hand by the economist Fred Gottheil (Middle East Quarterly), wrote of Muslim immigration that he was unable to even guess the size of total immigration. A letter by Ronald Sanders in the New York Review of Books, written in defence of Joan Peters's thesis, says the British kept thorough records of Jewish immigration but none for Arabs migrating overland.

contested.text: Joan Peters's 1984 book argued that much Arab growth was illegal immigration drawn by Zionist prosperity. Later reviewers stressed its technical, historical and literary faults; Daniel Pipes, who had praised it, does not dispute the faults but holds that neither Yehoshua Porath nor any other reviewer has refuted its central thesis. Porath, an Israeli historian (quoted here second-hand, in a letter by Ronald Sanders), held that most of the growth was natural increase, as the British and UN inquiries had found. The economist Fred Gottheil argues that unrecorded illegal immigration from 1922 to 1931 mattered. Our reading: the large majority of the growth was natural increase; some immigration and movement within the country happened but cannot be measured.

could_not_verify: The end-of-1946 figures: UNSCOP and the Mandate government's 1947 Supplement to the Survey (reproduced in a 1949 UN paper, whose scan is garbled) are the documents; the Supplement itself was not found online. I found no independent scholar or news page that repeats the Arab and Jewish split.

The Survey of Palestine and the Anglo-American report give the Jewish and Arab counts but differ in total (1,765,000 vs 1,727,786 in the American Jewish Year Book) because of how they count forces and nomads; I did not resolve it.
UNSCOP's own table of religions gives a 1922 Muslim figure (486,177) that does not match the census (590,890); I cite only its prose paragraphs.
I did not find a readable page by a demographer arguing that Arab growth from 1922 to 1946 was mostly immigration other than Gottheil on 1922-1931.

Every count from 1922 on (the 1922 and 1931 census reports, the Survey, the Anglo-American Committee, UNSCOP, Hansard) is one set of Mandate statistics. The record facts rest on the document itself; the two confirming sources check that we read it right, they are not independent measurements. Facts 5, 7, 9, 10 and 11 are the weakest on this point.

The 1922 census report scan (hosted by Australian National University) is poorly OCR-ed: its table of religions is unreadable, so the breakdown by religion rests on the Economic Cooperation Foundation page, the Report on Palestine Administration 1922 and the 1931 report's comparison table; the quote on the card is the report's own sentence, copied with its OCR errors.

Justin McCarthy's book The Population of Palestine (1990) is the standard study of Ottoman undercounting in Palestine; no page of it was readable here. The card cites his statement from a paper on the Ottoman Armenians, which says the Ottomans consistently undercounted women and children across the empire. What a person needs to read: McCarthy, The Population of Palestine, chapters 1 and 2 (Columbia University Press, 1990), or Roberto Bachi, The Population of Israel (1977), pp. 4-5.

Fact 6 (the 1948 British written answer) is kept as one record with no confirming source: the other Jewish-population figures on the card are for different dates. Fact 11 has one reliable source besides the Survey (a letter in a magazine, written in defence of Peters's thesis); a first-hand demographer on unrecorded Arab immigration (Bachi in his own book) was not readable.

Pre-1914 estimates (275,000 in 1800, over half a million in 1890) rest on DellaPergola, who rests on Bachi, McEvedy and Jones, and Dulska; I did not find a second readable page that gives its own estimate for 1800.

Fact 6 (British figures given to Parliament in 1939 and 1948) has two government records and one news report (on a different basis, the Jewish National Fund count); I found no second reliable page that repeats the 1923 and 1948 figures. Fact 11 has one reliable source besides the Survey (a letter in a magazine, written in defence of Peters's thesis); a first-hand demographer on unrecorded Arab immigration (Bachi in his own book) was not readable.

Round two reviewer: record facts 4, 5, 6, 7, 9, 10 and 11 do not have two readers who report the same content. Fact 4: only the Anglo-American Committee repeats the 1,765,000 (the Year Book gives a different estimate). Fact 5: the 1949 UN paper is a garbled reproduction of a different record and DellaPergola's 1947 figures are rounded and a different date. Fact 6: both Hansard answers are records and the JNF count is a different thing. Fact 7: UNSCOP, the Anglo-American Committee and the Survey each give a different number. Facts 9, 10: the three sources are three records, and the Survey quote in fact 9 is a cut sentence.
not_claimed: This card does not say there was no Arab immigration into Palestine, only that the official inquiries put it at a small share of the growth.
It does not say the Jewish population was small in 1947; it says it was about a third.
It does not give the Arab population by origin or say how many Arab families were in their villages for generations.
It does not say the land was 'empty' or 'full': counts alone do not settle that.

skeptic.notes: Round two, after the record rule. Read the is_record scans: 1922 report (ANU scan, poor OCR: 757,182 and the erratum 83,694 to 83,794 are legible; the Bedouin of Beersheba were estimated, not counted), 1931 Table VII (1,035,821; settled 969,288; Jews 174,610), Survey, UNSCOP, Hansard (both answers). Figures match their records; wording of record facts is 'the report records', not 'there were'. [must-fix] Readers: facts 2 and 3 have real readers (Administration report, ECF, JTA; ECF, Emory). Facts 4, 5, 6, 7, 9, 10, 11 do not: fact 4 only the Anglo-American Committee repeats 1,765,000, and the Year Book's own table for 1944 is 1,727,786 with 521,564 Jews (now said on the card; the Survey's 554,000 is a revised de facto figure); fact 5 has no source repeating the Arab/Jewish split (DellaPergola is rounded 1947); fact 6 both Hansard answers are records and JNF is another count; facts 7, 9, 10 cite three different records, each saying something different, so none confirms another; fact 9's Survey quote is a cut sentence. The writer's own notes admit this. [must-fix] Fact 6 wording was garbled ('in 1939, about 58,000 Jews ... in 1919'); rewritten by date of each answer. Fact 0 said Ottoman counts undercounted; the Cambridge article found the Ottoman count higher than usual estimates, so only 'the older outside estimates may be too low' and McCarthy's empire-wide statement are claimed. [should-fix] Fact 1: one source per estimate (689,000 only the Survey); a duplicate source entry removed. Fact 2 did not say the Bedouin were estimated; fact 3 did not say its total includes nomads. Heard (Khalidi on 1948) is not about population. Missing first-hand demographer (McCarthy's Palestine book, Bachi) remains. Honest handling of the first-round must-fix (one dataset): stated in fact 5 and the answer. Strongest objections: Palestinian side, no first-hand demographer on the Ottoman undercount of Palestine; Israeli side, the 1944 Jewish figure varies by 33,000 between estimates.

citer.notes: Round two after the record rule. Answer re-split into 8 sentences, each tied to facts. Reworded 'Ottoman counts undercounted' (not shown for Palestine) to 'some were probably undercounts' (fact 0). The 12.91/32.96 percent sentence is carried by fact 5 (UNSCOP's own table, like with like). 'Every count after 1922 is one set of Mandate statistics' is carried by fact 5's text. Sentences are supported by the facts as worded; the readers behind those facts are the weakness, not the tie.
